Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI

Sergey Shirobokov Affiliation: Google DeepMind    Ben Jaderberg Affiliation: Google DeepMind    Katerina Hristova    George Tsoukalas Affiliation: Google DeepMind    Johannes Bausch Affiliation: Google DeepMind    Eric Wieser  Affiliation: Google DeepMind    Francisco J.H. Heras Affiliation: Google DeepMind    Nicholas C. Rubin Affiliation: Google Quantum AI    Guang Hao Low Affiliation: Google Quantum AI    Sébastien Racanière Affiliation: Google DeepMind    Nenad Tomašev Affiliation: Google DeepMind    Lei M. Zhang Affiliation: Google DeepMind    James Watson Affiliation: Google Quantum AI    Tanuj Khattar Affiliation: Google Quantum AI    Aws Albarghouthi    Stavan Jain    Harun Khan Affiliation: Google DeepMind    Leopoldo Sarra Affiliation: Google DeepMind    Andrew W. Senior Affiliation: Google DeepMind    Michael Broughton Affiliation: Google Quantum AI    Hussain Masoom Affiliation: Google DeepMind    Sergio Boixo Affiliation: Google Quantum AI    Ryan Babbush Affiliation: Google Quantum AI    Swarat Chaudhuri Affiliation: Google DeepMind    Pushmeet Kohli Affiliation: Google DeepMind
November 6, 2026
Abstract

The timeline by which quantum computers can solve breakthrough problems in science depends on improved quantum algorithms as much as on better hardware [148, 149]. Such algorithmic advances are typically achieved through many years of expert human collaboration [150, 151]. In mathematics and computer science, large language models have accelerated progress through automated discovery loops [152, 153]. However, quantum algorithms can only be evaluated by classical computers on restricted or small instances [154, 155]. Here we demonstrate automated discovery of quantum programs beyond these regimes including order-of-magnitude improvements on scientific applications. To achieve this, we build a quantum program library in the Lean theorem prover in which large language model agents synthesize novel programs against formal problem specifications and verify their correctness and cost. Agent teams collaborate, sharing results and knowledge through wikis and discussing ideas at organized conferences. Our results improve on prior baselines for parallel search [156] (up to 1.4×1.4\times), quantum arithmetic [157] (290×290\times), and simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug-metabolism by 11×11\times, 8×8\times and 2.5×2.5\times respectively. Combining human and artificial intelligence at scale, under the rigor of mathematical proof, lets researchers design algorithms that today’s classical and quantum computers cannot test, shortening the path to practical quantum computation.
